summary: At Ephesus Paul meets disciples acquainted only with John's baptism. They receive instruction, baptism in Jesus's name, Paul's hands, the Holy Spirit, tongues, and prophecy. After synagogue resistance Paul teaches daily in the school of Tyrannus for two years, so the word reaches the province of Asia. Extraordinary healings prompt itinerant exorcists to use Jesus's name as a technique, but a possessed man overwhelms the seven sons of Sceva. Fear, confession, and the burning of costly magic books accompany the word's growth. Because Paul's mission threatens the Artemis-image trade, Demetrius turns economic loss into civic-religious outrage; a huge theater crowd chants until the town clerk calms them through legal procedure.
whyItMatters: Ephesus exposes rival ways of understanding power. The Spirit is received in relationship to Jesus, not through an isolated formula; Jesus's name cannot be commercially or magically manipulated; costly renunciation follows confession; and idolatry is upheld by an economic network as well as belief. The word becomes ‘mighty’ without Christians seizing the city or desecrating its shrine.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator presenting the third mission's long Ephesian center
context.audience: Readers navigating baptism, Spirit, magic, public religion, economics, and civic conflict
context.date: Paul's Ephesian ministry is commonly placed in the early-to-mid 50s
context.setting: Ephesus, capital of Roman Asia, with synagogue, lecture hall, households, marketplace, and theater
context.literaryForm: Instruction and Spirit-reception scene, ministry summary, failed-exorcism caution, conversion report, and civic riot

outline.heading: Twelve disciples receive fuller instruction, baptism, and the Spirit
Daily teaching and extraordinary works spread the word through Asia
Failed magical use of Jesus's name leads to confession and renunciation
The Artemis economy erupts into a confused civic assembly

keyVerses.text: He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
keyVerses.why: The question exposes an incomplete initiation centered only on John's preparatory baptism.

keyVerses.text: So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.
keyVerses.why: The narrator portrays the word—not magic, money, or Paul—as the force gaining strength.

keyVerses.text: You see and hear that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods that are made with hands.
keyVerses.why: Demetrius unintentionally summarizes the mission's reach and its economic-theological threat.

questions.question: Who are the twelve ‘disciples,’ and what had they not heard?
questions.answer: They know John's baptism but lack teaching about the Holy Spirit's arrival in relation to Jesus. Their statement can mean they had not heard that the Spirit ‘was given’ rather than no knowledge of the Spirit's existence at all. Acts calls them disciples before fuller instruction, showing an incomplete transitional group rather than easy categories.

questions.question: Does this episode establish one required order for baptism and Spirit reception?
questions.answer: They hear fuller proclamation, are baptized in Jesus's name, receive Paul's laying on hands, and then speak in tongues and prophesy. Other Acts scenes order these elements differently. Here the sequence publicly links John's preparatory ministry, Jesus, apostolic witness, and the Spirit; it should be compared with all the narratives before becoming a universal test.

questions.question: What is ‘the Way’ in the Ephesian dispute?
questions.answer: Acts again uses hē hodos as a public name for the Jesus movement and its manner of life. When some become hardened and speak evil of ‘the Way,’ Paul relocates the disciples rather than letting synagogue conflict define the whole mission. The phrase will also be used by Demetrius for the economically disruptive movement.

questions.question: What was the school of Tyrannus?
questions.answer: Scholē can mean a lecture hall or school, and Tyrannus may be an owner or teacher. Paul uses it daily after leaving the synagogue. Some later manuscripts add teaching hours from late morning to afternoon, a vivid but probably secondary detail. The critical text supports sustained public instruction without preserving a timetable.

questions.question: Are handkerchief healings an endorsement of relic commerce?
questions.answer: Luke labels the works ‘special miracles’ through Paul and reports cloths associated with his labor reaching the sick. The next story immediately condemns treating Jesus's name as a manipulable technique. Whatever view readers take of material mediation, Acts gives no permission to commercialize objects or detach healing from God's initiative.

questions.question: Why do the sons of Sceva fail if they say Jesus's name?
questions.answer: They invoke ‘Jesus whom Paul preaches’ as a borrowed exorcistic formula, not as commissioned witnesses. The spirit distinguishes knowing Jesus and Paul from not recognizing them, then overpowers them. Acts' theology of the name is relational and authoritative, never verbal magic.

questions.question: Why burn the books instead of selling them?
questions.answer: The converts publicly confess practices and destroy manuals whose reuse would perpetuate magic. Luke emphasizes the enormous cost—fifty thousand silver pieces—to show repentance disrupting economic value. The event is voluntary action by practitioners concerning their own materials, not authorization for coercive censorship or burning other people's books.

questions.question: How does Demetrius turn profit anxiety into religious patriotism?
questions.answer: He first names the craftspeople's wealth, then says Paul's teaching discredits handmade gods, then warns that Artemis's temple and worldwide magnificence will be despised. Economic interest, civic identity, religious devotion, and masculine trade solidarity reinforce one another. The crowd's chant hides the original balance sheet behind honor for the goddess.

questions.question: What does the confused assembly reveal about crowd power?
questions.answer: Many participants do not know why they gathered; competing groups shout, Paul's friends restrain him, and anti-Jewish hostility redirects attention when Alexander appears. The town clerk finally appeals to uncontested civic facts and lawful courts. Acts neither endorses mob rule nor depicts Christian witness as destruction of temples—the clerk says the missionaries are not shrine robbers or blasphemers.

glossary.def: Capital of Roman Asia and major center of Artemis worship, commerce, and travel.
Name associated with the lecture hall where Paul taught daily.
Ephesian patron goddess whose great temple anchored religious identity and economic activity.
